newsitem.title: UK: Prospective UK Chancellors square up in TV debate.
newsitem.headline: Prospective UK Chancellors square up in TV debate.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and his Labour counterpart Gordon Brown clashed in a televised debate on Sunday but ended up sounding remarkably similar on a whole range of issues.

In the first three-way debate of the 1997 election campaign between leading members of the main political parties -- Liberal Democrat finance spokesman Malcolm Bruce made up the trio -- it was difficult to detect much difference over tax, spending or Europe between the big two.
Clarke, of the ruling Conservatives, accused Brown of making policy over a single European currency "on the hoof" but they showed few differences over European economic and monetary union.

Clarke said he would not join EMU unless European Union economies had converged properly, while Brown said: "All of us agree there are considerable obstacles. All of us agree that at the moment, for many countries, it is highly unlikely."
Brown said the national economic interest was the test for joining or not and Clarke said Britain should exercise its option to opt out of a single currency on the basis of its economic interest.
Labour, 20 points or more ahead in the opinion polls, looks poised to take power for the first time in 18 years in the May 1 elections.

But in many instances, it was hard to slide a cigarette paper between the policies proposed by Brown and Clarke. Both said they would not raise tax in the next parliament but managed a heated debate just the same.

"There is no reason whatsoever to raise taxation," Clarke said. "It would take exceptional events to drive us back into raising taxation and those exceptional events are not seen by any sensible commentator."
Brown, who has pledged to leave the standard and top rates of income tax unchanged, challenged Clarke to explain how he would pary for tax cuts promised in the Conservative manifesto.
Clarke said improvements in the public finances would fund the Conservative pledge to reduce tax for some married couples.

Brown has promised to match Conservative spending plans for the next two years and said every Labour policy was properly costed. Clarke repeated his allegation of a 12 billion pounds hole in Labour's plans.

Brown dodged a question on whether interest rates would be put up early under a Labour government. But he backed a 2.5 percent target for underlying inflation, the same figure that Clarke has adopted.

Clarke, who meets Bank of England Governor Eddie George this week to discuss monetary policy, said his difference of opinion with George on interests rates amounted to just 1/4 of a percentage point. George has pressed for a base rate increase.

Bruce of the Liberal Democrats offered perhaps the most radical agenda, promising to raise income tax by a penny in the pound to fund improvements in health and education and pledging to make the Bank of England independent.
The media has been clamouring for a televised debate between the party leaders but, after inter-party wrangling over the details, this now looks unlikely to happen.

If Sunday's stand-off was anything to go by, the watching public may breathe a huge sigh of relief. "There was nothing new in any of that," a Labour source said. "All it shows is the format doesn't work."
